subject: Arabic (Optional)
content: The Arabic alphabet has 28 letters. It is written from right to left. The letters change shape depending on their position in a word (isolated, beginning, middle, end). Key letters: Alif (ا), Baa (ب), Taa (ت), Thaa (ث), Jeem (ج), Haa (ح), Khaa (خ), Daal (د), Thaal (ذ), Raa (ر), Zay (ز), Seen (س), Sheen (ش), Saad (ص), Daad (ض), Taa (ط), Dhaa (ظ), Ayn (ع), Ghayn (غ), Faa (ف), Qaaf (ق), Kaaf (ك), Laam (ل), Meem (م), Noon (ن), Ha (ه), Waw (و), Yaa (ي). Arabic has sounds not found in English like ع (Ayn) and غ (Ghayn). Practice writing and pronouncing each letter. Arabic is the language of the Quran and is spoken by millions in Nigeria, especially in northern states.
summary: Arabic alphabet has 28 letters written right to left. Letters change shape based on position. Includes unique sounds like ع and غ. Important in northern Nigeria.

subject: Arabic (Optional)
content: Arabic greetings are important in Islamic culture. As-salamu alaykum (السلام عليكم) means 'Peace be upon you' - the most common greeting. Response: Wa alaykum as-salam (وعليكم السلام) - 'And upon you be peace'. Good morning: Sabah al-khayr (صباح الخير). Response: Sabah an-nur (صباح النور). Good evening: Masa al-khayr (مساء الخير). Response: Masa an-nur (مساء النور). Hello: Marhaba (مرحبا). How are you? (to male): Kayfa haluka? (كيف حالك؟), (to female): Kayfa haluki? (كيف حالك؟). Response: Ana bikhayr, shukran (أنا بخير شكرا) - 'I am fine, thank you'. Goodbye: Ma'a as-salamah (مع السلامة). Thank you: Shukran (شكرا). You're welcome: Afwan (عفوا). Yes: Na'am (نعم). No: La (لا). In Nigerian Muslim communities, these greetings are used daily.
summary: Common Arabic greetings: As-salamu alaykum (Peace be upon you), Sabah al-khayr (Good morning), Shukran (Thank you), Ma'a as-salamah (Goodbye).

subject: Arabic (Optional)
content: Learning Arabic numbers helps with counting and Islamic prayers. Numbers 1-10: 1 = Wahid (واحد), 2 = Ithnan (اثنان), 3 = Thalatha (ثلاثة), 4 = Arba'a (أربعة), 5 = Khamsa (خمسة), 6 = Sitta (ستة), 7 = Sab'a (سبعة), 8 = Thamaniya (ثمانية), 9 = Tis'a (تسعة), 10 = Ashara (عشرة). These numbers are used in daily life, telling time, and understanding ages. In Nigerian Quranic schools, children learn to count in Arabic alongside English. Practice counting objects, reciting numbers after prayers, and using them in simple sentences.
summary: Arabic numbers 1-10: wahid, ithnan, thalatha, arba'a, khamsa, sitta, sab'a, thamaniya, tis'a, ashara.

subject: Arabic (Optional)
content: Family members in Arabic: father = Ab (أب), mother = Umm (أم), brother = Akh (أخ), sister = Ukht (أخت), son = Ibn (ابن), daughter = Bint (بنت), grandfather = Jadd (جد), grandmother = Jaddah (جدة), uncle = Amm or Kha (عم or خال), aunt = Ammah or Khala (عمة or خالة), cousin = Ibn Amm etc., husband = Zawj (زوج), wife = Zawjah (زوجة). Using possessive: Abi (my father), Ummi (my mother), Akhi (my brother), Ukhti (my sister). In Arabic culture, family is very important and extended family often lives together. In northern Nigeria, family terms are used not just for relatives but also for close community members as a sign of respect.
summary: Family in Arabic: Ab (father), Umm (mother), Akh (brother), Ukht (sister), Ibn (son), Bint (daughter), Jadd (grandfather), Jaddah (grandmother).

subject: Arabic (Optional)
content: Colors in Arabic: red = Ahmar (أحمر), blue = Azraq (أزرق), green = Akhdar (أخضر), yellow = Asfar (أصفر), black = Aswad (أسود), white = Abyad (أبيض), brown = Bunni (بني), pink = Wardiy (وردي), purple = Banafsaji (بنفسجي), orange = Burtuqali (برتقالي). Color agreement: In Arabic, colors change form depending on the gender of the noun. For masculine: Ahmar, Azraq, Akhdar. For feminine: Hamra, Zarqa, Khadra. Example: Bayt ahmar (red house - masculine), Sayyarah hamra (red car - feminine). Colors are used to describe objects, clothing, and nature. In Islamic art, green is a significant color representing paradise.
summary: Arabic colors: Ahmar (red), Azraq (blue), Akhdar (green), Aswad (black), Abyad (white). Colors change for feminine nouns: Hamra, Zarqa, Khadra.

subject: Arabic (Optional)
content: Arabic vocabulary for Islamic prayers. The five daily prayers: Fajr (dawn), Dhuhr (noon), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (sunset), Isha (night). Prayer parts: Takbir (Allahu Akbar - God is greatest), Ruku (bowing), Sujud (prostration), Tashahhud (sitting testimony), Salam (greeting of peace). Common phrases: Bismillah (In the name of God), Alhamdulillah (Praise be to God), Subhanallah (Glory be to God), Astaghfirullah (I seek forgiveness from God), Insha'Allah (God willing), Masha'Allah (God has willed it). In Nigeria, Muslim children learn these phrases from a young age in Quranic schools (Tsangaya or Almajiri system).
summary: Prayer vocabulary: Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, Isha. Phrases: Allahu Akbar, Bismillah, Alhamdulillah, Subhanallah, Insha'Allah.

quiz_questions.subject: Arabic (Optional)
quiz_questions.content: Days of the week in Arabic: Monday = Al-Ithnayn (الاثنين), Tuesday = Al-Thulatha (الثلاثاء), Wednesday = Al-Arba'a (الأربعاء), Thursday = Al-Khamis (الخميس), Friday = Al-Jumu'ah (الجمعة), Saturday = Al-Sabt (السبت), Sunday = Al-Ahad (الأحد). Friday (Al-Jumu'ah) is the holy day for Muslims, when special congregational prayers are held. In Nigeria, many businesses close early on Fridays for Jumu'ah prayers. The Arabic week starts with Sunday (Al-Ahad) or Monday (Al-Ithnayn) depending on context. Practice saying the days and using them in sentences about weekly activities.
quiz_questions.summary: Days: Al-Ahad (Sun), Al-Ithnayn (Mon), Al-Thulatha (Tue), Al-Arba'a (Wed), Al-Khamis (Thu), Al-Jumu'ah (Fri), Al-Sabt (Sat). Friday is holy day.

quiz_questions.subject: Arabic (Optional)
quiz_questions.content: Common Arabic phrases used daily by Muslims worldwide. Greetings: As-salamu alaykum (Peace be upon you), Response: Wa alaykum as-salam. Thank you: Shukran. You're welcome: Afwan. Please: Min fadlik (to male), Min fadliki (to female). Excuse me / Sorry: Afwan or Aasif. Yes: Na'am. No: La. OK: Hasan. Good: Jayyid. Very good: Jayyid jiddan. Congratulations: Mubarak. Blessings: Barakallah. In Nigeria, these phrases are commonly used among Muslims regardless of their native language. Learning these phrases helps in communicating with Arabic-speaking visitors and understanding Islamic culture.
quiz_questions.summary: Common Arabic phrases: Shukran (thank you), Afwan (you're welcome), Min fadlik (please), Na'am (yes), La (no), Mubarak (congratulations).
